endorsements.quote: A designated executive owner should be accountable for the service from patient entry to outcome and remedy, while professional and statutory duties remain with those who hold them.
Thresholds for action, ranging from investigation and workflow change to retraining, restriction, rollback, suspension, or termination, should be agreed before problems arise.

Where authority is distributed across organizations in this way, accountability can be shared through a written agreement that assigns each function to a named party, sets escalation routes, and gives the lead organization the right to obtain information and require corrective action from its partners.

Contracts should require vendors to provide performance and safety evidence, allow audits, notify the organization of material changes, cooperate with incident investigations, return data in a usable format, delete data securely when required, and support an orderly suspension or exit.
A current register should record, for each clinically consequential component, its owner, intended use, supporting evidence, version, dependencies, incidents, complaints, and outcomes.
Any material change to the data, model, interface, or workflow should send the service back through the risk gate.
Reviews should ask whether harms recur, whether performance differs across patient groups, and whether patterns of accepted recommendations and overrides point to risk.

Services need tested downtime and exit plans, and patients need one accessible route through which the responsible organization investigates, explains what happened, corrects records, hears appeals, and provides remedy.
Table 1 illustrates how assurance could scale with the clinical influence of each AI function, from administrative support to tools that inform diagnosis or treatment.
Where even these are not feasible, the minimum is a named owner, a defined pathway with confirmed referral, and an agreed point at which the service will be paused.
Equity has to be assessed before and during operation, including for people who never complete an encounter.
Governance costs belong in the service budget, and services should be launched only where the health system can monitor and support them.
AI audit logs; override records; monthly and after each model or interface change
Clinicians need to know what the tool is for and where it tends to fail, be able to override it, and know how to report concerns.

unlisted_practices: Ensure patients can decline AI-supported telemedicine steps without losing care.
Make clear to patients when AI is involved in their care.
Involve patients and community representatives in telemedicine service design.
Provide language and disability access in telemedicine services.
Implement closed-loop escalation and referral confirming the receiving service accepts responsibility and the patient reaches appropriate care.
Define clear clinical pathway rules covering remote management scope, red flags, identity, consent, prescribing, and in-person assessment triggers.
Practice continuing data stewardship with purpose specification, lawful basis, data minimization, retention limits, and limits on secondary use rather than relying on consent alone.
Integrate cybersecurity into clinical governance for AI-enabled telemedicine.
Use an existing quality or patient safety committee to take on the AI review role where resources are limited.
Provide standard contract clauses, shared registers, and pooled clinical review at ministry level to reduce burden on individual facilities.
Use simpler data sources such as sampled telephone follow-up and referral confirmation where records cannot be linked.
Do not use safety dashboards to rank services against each other.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/discussion paper proposing a practical leadership and governance framework for AI-enabled telemedicine in LMICs.
